headline: 3 easy
steps
process.support: Collect at home. Send it back. See your results, clearly explained.
process.instructions: Follow the instructions supplied with your kit.

steps.title: Virtually painless. At home.
steps.body: Your kit comes to you. Collect a small blood sample from your upper arm with Tasso+. No needles to handle.
steps.detail: Press once and release. Allow up to 5 minutes.

steps.title: Send it back. Prepaid.
steps.body: Protect your sample as instructed and send it to the laboratory in the prepaid return envelope.

steps.title: Your results. Clearly explained.
steps.body: Open EVA to see your results, understand what each marker measures, and begin building your own health history.
steps.detail: Results in 2 working days from laboratory receipt of your sample.

timing.qualifier: From laboratory receipt of your sample.

process.transition: And this is what you get back.
process.designerIntent: Preserve the approved continuous film. Step text should guide the eye, not become an instruction manual. End on the same EVA interface introduced in the next section.

headline: Your results.
Clearly explained.
results.support: See what each biomarker measures, how your result relates to the laboratory range, and how it compares with your own past readings.

annotations.title: Understand the result.

annotations.detail: A plain-language explanation gives each abbreviation a purpose.

annotations.title: Put it in perspective.

annotations.detail: Ranges are part of the picture. Interpretation also depends on your circumstances.

annotations.title: Follow your own history.

annotations.detail: Your first reading is a baseline. Later comparable readings help you see the pattern.

starting.title: You don't need to speak lab.

results.detailNote: Examples illustrate the interface. A blood result is one part of your health picture and should be read in context.
results.transition: Start with the signals in this kit.
results.designerIntent: Use the actual EVA dashboard design. Keep approved kit markers and honest example labels in focus. Do not headline unsupported score or biological-age estimates.

headline: 13 markers.
A clearer starting point.
panel.support: Explore blood fats, recent blood sugar, inflammation, and markers related to your liver and kidneys. Learn what each result can add to the picture.
panel.helper: Choose an area to see what is included.

groups.label: Heart & lipids
groups.description: Four measurements that help put your blood fats in perspective.
groups.detail: Read total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides together. Each adds context to the wider lipid profile.

groups.label: Blood sugar
groups.description: A view of your recent average blood sugar.
groups.detail: Fructosamine reflects glucose attached to blood proteins, offering a view over roughly the previous two to three weeks.

groups.label: Inflammation
groups.description: A sensitive measurement of a protein linked to inflammation.
groups.detail: hs-CRP measures small amounts of C-reactive protein. The result needs context; it does not identify the cause of inflammation on its own.

groups.label: Liver & protein
groups.description: Protein and enzyme measurements that make more sense together.
groups.detail: Albumin, ALP, ALT and GGT contribute different information. They are interpreted alongside one another and your circumstances.

groups.label: Kidney-related markers
groups.description: Measurements connected with waste production and clearance.
groups.detail: Creatinine and urea BUN are commonly used in kidney assessment. Uric acid adds information about a different waste product and its clearance.

markers.name: Albumin
markers.short: A key protein made by your liver.
markers.detail: Albumin helps transport substances in your blood and maintain fluid balance. Read it alongside other results and your circumstances.

markers.name: ALP
markers.short: An enzyme found in the liver, bile ducts and bone.
markers.detail: ALP is often read with other liver-related tests. Its level can reflect more than one tissue, so context matters.

markers.name: hs-CRP
markers.short: A sensitive measurement of a protein linked to inflammation.
markers.detail: CRP can change with inflammation, infection or injury. One result does not explain the cause on its own.

markers.name: Creatinine
markers.short: A muscle-related waste product filtered by your kidneys.
markers.detail: Creatinine contributes to kidney assessment. Muscle mass, activity and other factors can influence the result.

markers.name: Urea BUN
markers.short: A measurement related to protein breakdown and waste clearance.
markers.detail: Urea nitrogen is carried in the blood and cleared by the kidneys. It is commonly considered alongside creatinine and other context.

markers.name: Uric acid
markers.short: A waste product formed when your body breaks down purines.
markers.detail: Your body produces uric acid and clears much of it through the kidneys. A result reflects both production and clearance.

markers.name: Total cholesterol
markers.short: An overall measurement of cholesterol in your blood.
markers.detail: The total is one part of the lipid profile. LDL, HDL and triglycerides add information that a total alone cannot provide.

markers.name: LDL Cholesterol
markers.short: The cholesterol carried in LDL particles.
markers.detail: LDL is one part of a cardiovascular risk assessment. It is interpreted with the rest of your lipid results and health context.

markers.name: HDL-Cholesterol
markers.short: The cholesterol carried in HDL particles.
markers.detail: HDL helps transport cholesterol. Read the value as part of your wider lipid profile rather than as an isolated score.

markers.name: Triglycerides
markers.short: A type of fat carried in your blood.
markers.detail: Triglycerides contribute to the lipid picture alongside total cholesterol, LDL and HDL.

markers.name: ALT
markers.short: An enzyme found mainly in liver cells.
markers.detail: ALT is commonly included in liver-related blood tests and interpreted alongside other measurements.

markers.name: GGT
markers.short: An enzyme used in liver and bile-duct assessment.
markers.detail: GGT can help put other liver-related results, including ALP, into context.

markers.name: Fructosamine
markers.short: A view of average blood sugar over the past 2–3 weeks.
markers.detail: This measures glucose attached to blood proteins. Albumin levels and other factors can affect interpretation.

panel.footer: The right reading brings measurements and context together. Individual markers do not diagnose a condition on their own.
panel.designerIntent: Give the five areas room to breathe, with all13names discoverable. Let a selected marker reveal one useful explanation. Do not bury the exact kit contents behind purely decorative animation.
